planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top of the rhizome exposed at the soil surface in well-drained, average soil in full sun; bearded iris rots quickly if planted too deep or kept in soggy soil.

directions: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top of the rhizome exposed at the soil surface in well-drained, average soil in full sun; bearded iris rots quickly if planted too deep or kept in soggy soil. Ruffled, richly textured flowers combine deep burgundy-purple standards with lighter, veined falls edged in a lace-like ruffle, a bold, dramatic bicolor combination typical of modern award-winning bearded iris breeding, blooming on tall, sturdy stems in late spring. Like other tall bearded iris, it thrives in lean to average soil with excellent drainage, needing full sun and no more than light fertilizing to bloom well, and multiplies steadily by rhizome division over several years. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in late summer, discarding the older central rhizomes and replanting only vigorous outer divisions, and keep the rhizome tops exposed to sun to prevent rot.

directions: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top of the rhizome exposed at the soil surface in well-drained, average soil in full sun; bearded iris rots quickly if planted too deep or kept in soggy soil. Large, luminous, blended flowers move through soft tones of lavender, blue, and cream across each ruffled petal, a subtle, ethereal color blend that gives the cultivar an almost glowing quality in the garden, opening on tall, well-branched stems in late spring. Bred for strong garden performance and reliable rebloom potential in favorable climates, it is a well-regarded modern tall bearded iris that multiplies readily into a substantial clump within a few seasons of planting. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in late summer, replanting only the youngest, most vigorous rhizomes, and keep the rhizome top exposed to sun to prevent rot.

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top of the rhizome exposed at the soil surface in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Gnu Again is a reblooming iris that flowers again in late summer or fall in climates with a long enough growing season.

directions: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top of the rhizome exposed at the soil surface in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Gnu Again is a reblooming iris that flowers again in late summer or fall in climates with a long enough growing season. Creamy yellow standards contrast with white falls delicately edged in the same soft yellow, a clean, cheerful color combination on a dependable, award-winning reblooming bearded iris that, given a sufficiently long and mild growing season, produces a second flush of bloom in late summer or fall beyond the typical single spring display. Reblooming iris cultivars generally need consistent moisture and a light feeding after the first spring bloom to support the energy demands of a second flowering cycle, performing best in climates with long, warm falls rather than an early hard frost. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in late summer, and keep rhizome tops exposed to sun to prevent rot.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained to consistently moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Siberian iris tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and needs no rhizome exposure at planting.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained to consistently moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Siberian iris tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and needs no rhizome exposure at planting. Crisp white falls contrast sharply with clear butter-yellow standards, a clean two-tone combination that has made this one of the most enduringly popular Siberian iris cultivars since its introduction decades ago, blooming above narrow, grass-like foliage that stays attractive well after flowering finishes. Unlike bearded iris, Siberian iris grows from a fibrous root system rather than a rhizome, tolerates moist to average soil without rotting, and is essentially pest- and disease-free, making it one of the lowest-maintenance perennials for a sunny border or pond-adjacent planting. Divide congested clumps every four to five years in early spring or fall, and cut foliage back in late fall or early spring before new growth begins.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in wet to consistently moist, acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Japanese iris wants more moisture than bearded iris and benefits from standing in shallow water briefly during its spring growing season.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in wet to consistently moist, acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Japanese iris wants more moisture than bearded iris and benefits from standing in shallow water briefly during its spring growing season. Crisply white-striped, sword-shaped leaves provide months of bright variegated texture before the classic large, flat, deep reddish-purple Japanese iris flowers open in early summer, a striking foliage-and-flower combination that extends the ornamental season well beyond the relatively brief bloom period typical of the species. Native to wet meadows and marsh edges across East Asia, it wants acidic, consistently moist to wet soil unlike the drier, alkaline conditions bearded iris prefers, making it a good companion for the wet margin of a pond or rain garden. Keep soil consistently moist through the growing season, avoid lime or alkaline amendments, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring or right after flowering.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; daylilies tolerate a wide range of soil conditions and need little care once established.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; daylilies tolerate a wide range of soil conditions and need little care once established. Large, elegantly ruffled flowers open in a soft, dusty lavender-orchid shade with a subtle deeper eyezone and a lightly ruffled gold edge, a refined pastel color combination that has made this classic mid-twentieth-century cultivar a long-standing favorite among daylily collectors and a parent behind many later lavender and purple-toned daylily hybrids. Reliable and easy-growing like other daylilies, it thrives in average garden soil with minimal care, tolerating heat, drought, and a range of soil types once established, and each flower lasts only a single day but is followed by a long succession of new blooms through its flowering season. Deadhead spent flowers and remove old bloom stalks after flowering finishes, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain vigor.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; daylilies tolerate a wide range of soil conditions and need little care once established. Vivid orange-red petals with a darker red eyezone and a bright greenish-yellow throat combine for a bold, fiery color display that lives up to the cultivar's name, opening on well-branched scapes that carry numerous buds for an extended bloom season on an established, well-grown clump. As with all daylilies, each individual flower lasts only a single day, but a healthy plant produces a steady daily succession of new blooms over several weeks, and this cultivar's strong, saturated color makes it a standout accent among softer pastel daylily companions. Deadhead spent blooms and remove finished flower scapes at the base, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to keep the planting vigorous.
